newsitem.title: USA: US ATTACHE REPORT - UK DEMAND FOR POULTRY RISING.
newsitem.headline: US ATTACHE REPORT - UK DEMAND FOR POULTRY RISING.

text.p: Here is a report prepared by an agricultural attache with the U.S. Embassy in London and released Monday by the U.S. Agriculture Department.
Attache reports are not considered official USDA data.

Driven by BSE-induced concerns consumer demand for poultry meat enjoyed a significant boost during 1996 to end the year 3.6 percent above 1995. Although domestic broiler production was able to partially respond to stronger demand, increased turkey meat purchases were satisfied by higher import volumes. A result of the increased output of white broiler meat was to raise the quantity of dark meat available for export.

While not of the same magnitude experienced in 1996, when ouput rose by 4.1 percent, forecasts are for further demand led production increases in broiler output in 1997 and 1998. However, as further rises in demand are likely to be for added-value and chicken portions, the market value will rise faster than volume. This trend toward parts is expected to benefit import volumes. At the same time, the increase in broiler production will release greater quantities of exportable dark meat.

The strong rate of growth (3.8 percent) in turkey demand during 1996 is unlikely to be repeated during 1997 mainly because of competition from the broiler sector. As a result turkey meat production is forecast to remain at levels similar to 1996. However, domestic producers are then expected to react to the comparatively high level of total demand by raising output in 1998.
Import and export volumes are expected to increase only marginally during 1997 and 1998: imports with demand for breast meat and exports with the availability of dark meat.

To the surprise of many commentators demand for shell eggs strengthened substantially during the second half of 1996 as consumers returned to this alternative protein source. This resulted in a calendar year rise of 3.4 percent in shell egg consumption during 1996. But, as with turkey meat, domestic producers were unable to respond to this shift in demand. This gap between domestic supply and demand was satisfied by increased imports and lower egg product exports. However, exports of shell eggs rose reflecting buoyant demand in Continental Europe.

Initial estimates for 1997 are for a slight increase in egg production during the first half of the year, with ouput easing during the latter part of 1997 as prices weaken reducing the production incentive. In the short to medium term demand for shell eggs and egg products is again likely to ease resulting in lower import demand. Similarly, exports are expected to fall as Continental demand eases.

Total poultry meat production rose by 3.5 percent during 1996 to 1.4 million mt, of which 1,064,000 was broiler meat, 293,000 mt turkey meat, 55,000 hen meat, 27,000 duck meat and 3,000 mt goose meat. The majority of the increase reflected higher broiler placings fueled by increased consumer demand caused by BSE concerns.

Industry sources expect more modest growth rates during 1997 and 1998 as consumer demand returns to near-trend increases. However, most of this future growth is likely to be in the broiler sector, where problems of chick sourcing due to Newcastle Disease (ND) outbreaks (especially in Northern Ireland, where many chicks are sourced) are expected to come to an end. Feed prices are currently around 10 percent below levels of a year ago (at BPS 178 per mt for a 15 percent protein growers ration) and are expected to follow a downward trend during the 1997/8 season. This is expected to assist poultry meat to remain competitive against other meats.

According to the Meat and Livestock Commission (MLC), chicken's share of the retail meat market rose 2 percent to 39 percent during 1996, while turkey's declined marginally to around 10 percent. The MLC estimates that poultry meat accounted for 41.2 percent of all household meat purchases in 1996, up from 39.7 percent in 1995. Of this, 31.8 percent was of chicken pieces, 45.8 percent was of whole chickens and 11.9 percent was of whole turkeys. Sales of further processed products of both species grew during 1996, a trend which is forecast to continue in 1997 and 1998.

In comparison, retail beef sales fell by 2.5 percent to 18.5 percent of all meat sales, mutton and lamb increased by 0.4 percent to 9.3 percent, pork rose from 13.9 percent in 1995 to 14.5 percent in 1996, and bacon increased by 0.3 percent to 14.5 percent.
(Source: MLC. Excludes offal and imported meat products.)

In expenditure terms, poultry meat accounted for 30.6 percent of household meat purchases during 1996 compared to 28.1 percent in 1995. Of this, 44.4 percent was on chicken parts, 33.7 percent on whole chickens, and 5.9 percent on whole turkeys.

Initial indications are that total consumption will rise by around 2.5 percent during 1997 and by an additional 2.1 perc ent in 1998. Given that the British public's buying habits are now not as influenced by the BSE scare, the driving forces behind the continued rise in poultry consumption remain the relative price of poultry meat compared to other meats and its "healthy image."

According to official figures, total imports of poultry meat reached 288,000 mt in 1996, a 15 percent increase on 1995. France supplied less chicken and turkey to the UK in 1996 as domestic French demand rose significantly due to the BSE scare. This gave the Netherlands the opportunity to develop its market share. Imports from the Irish Republic also increased. Third country suppliers, notably Brazil and Thailand increased their chicken shipments considerably giving third countries an import share of over 8.5 percent in 1996 compared to 2.4 percent in 1995.

Imports are expected to increase slightly during 1997 and 1998 as demand outpaces production. However, the potential for U.S. exports to the UK and other EU countries involves a satisfactory outcome to the U.S.-EU veterinary negotiations. In the absence of the availability of U.S. supplies, turkey parts, which are required by independent processors, are likely to be supplied by other countries.

Despite buoyant domestic demand in 1996, UK exports rose significantly, with exports of chicken to Hong Kong and Russia driving the increase. The rationale behind this boost to exports is that the UK market is primarily for breast meat, so any increase in domestic production results in greater export availability. So long as EU feed prices are not substantially higher than world price levels EU producers are effectively able to cross subsidize dark-meat exports from their sale of high-priced breast meat in the domestic market. This is because, when EU cereals prices are comparatively low, the conversion of variable poultry meat levies to fixed tariffs under the Uruguay Round provides a comparatively higher barrier to imports. When combined with non-tariff barriers, this allows EU producers to charge higher prices for breast meat in the domestic market.

In addition to dark meat the UK chicken industry has also sought to provide chicken feet to Hong Kong and other South East Asian markets. Hillsdown Holdings subsidiary Belwood Foods has Europe's first fully automated plant dedicated to stripping chicken feet. Output is estimated at 2.5 million pairs of feet per week, weighing around 100 mt. The company also ships recovered frozen poultry meat to Russia.

Increased domestic production during 1997 and 1998 is expected to add to export availability. First quarter trade data reveal Hong Kong as the major export destination for British poultry meat, with South Africa in second position. Commencing April 23, 1997 China placed a ban on British poultry for six months due to concerns over Newcastle Disease. If no further outbreaks are recorded shipments will be allowed again from the end of September.

Although broiler production increased by 4.1 percent in 1996, this was less than had originally been expected due to problems with chick sourcing as a result of Newcastle Disease outbreaks. The ND outbreak in Northern Ireland exacerbated the situation because the Province is a major supplier of hatching eggs to the rest of the UK. These supply problems have now dissipated and production, driven by continued demand growth, is forecast to increase by around 2.8 percent in 1997 and by around 2.4 percent in 1998.

According to industry sources, demand for broiler meat (especially breast meat) was substantial during 1996 driven by consumer concerns over BSE. However, with a comparatively tight EU market for poultry meat, imports actually fell and price became the limiting factor. MLC figures indicate that the retail price of poultry meat increased by 8.2 percent between March and September 1996. Consumption was therefore constrained, only increasing 3.3 percent. As the figures below indicate, the most significant increases in retail sales volumes were of frozen added value products (up 24.6 percent) and cooked products (up 22.7 percent). Sales of whole birds declined in volume (but not in value).

Total poultry meat consumption is initially forecast to grow by around 2.4 percent and by around 2.3 percent in 1997 and 1998 respectively. However, as demand increases are likely to be driven by further processed chicken and by chicken portions, the value of the market will rise faster than volume growth. This could benefit third country shipments of chapter 16 cooked chicken meat able to enter the EU at the tariff rate of 13.9 percent.

High demand in other member states reduced EU shipments to the UK by 7.3 percent but imports from third countries rose from around 4,000 mt in 1995 to around 16,000 in 1996. Shipments from Brazil and Thailand were responsible for most of this increase. In total, UK broiler meat imports slipped back slightly adding to upward price pressure. Intra-EU imports are expected to increase slightly during both 1997 and 1998, but the degree to which third country imports will be able to ease domestic price pressure is presently uncertain due to EU processing requirements.

For the reasons previously mentioned, UK broiler exports rose by 12.1 percent in 1996 as the rise in domestic output increased the supply of dark meat needing to be exported. This scenario is likely to continue during 1997 and 1998, unless domestic breast meat becomes less competitive compared to imported product and/or red meats. Thus, lower beef prices may actually increase the need for the EU to use export subsidies.
